questions.key_step: Write the three roots as \frac ar,a,ar: the product of the roots gives a at once and the sum then gives a quadratic in r.
questions.justification: Vieta plus G.P. parametrisation, one quadratic; routine chain, no insight.

questions.key_step: Multiply by the common ratio \frac12 and subtract twice: the quadratic-type numerators drop to an arithmetico-geometric series and then to a G.P.
questions.justification: Arithmetico-geometric series by double subtraction (or standard sums), several stages with exact arithmetic and no options.

questions.key_step: Move 2 across: x+10x^3+100x^5 is a G.P. in t=10x^2, which factorises the sextic.
questions.justification: Hidden G.P. in x+10x^3+100x^5 factorises the sextic; an unfamiliar trick, numerical answer, then conjugate-root reading.

questions.key_step: Divide through by 5^{100}; then f(n)+f(100-n)=1, so the terms pair off with sum 1 and the middle term is \frac12.
questions.justification: Pairing f(n)+f(100-n)=1 is a known symmetry trick, but must be seen; floor step adds a precision check.

questions.key_step: Put t=3^{2\sin2x}; the A.P. condition gives \frac t3+\frac{81}t=28, and \sin2x\le1 rejects the second root.
questions.justification: Substitution t=3^{2\sin2x}, quadratic, range check, G.P. sum: three routine steps.

questions.key_step: Vieta gives \text{H.M.}=\frac{3\alpha\beta\gamma}{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}=\frac13=\text{A.M.}, and A.M. \ge G.M. \ge H.M. forces equality.
questions.justification: Needs the A.M.-G.M.-H.M. equality insight for a cubic's roots plus Vieta; moderate idea availability.

questions.key_step: The relation says the terms form an A.P. with d=1; the even-placed terms form another A.P.
questions.justification: A.P. sum then sum of even terms; routine, only two linear steps.

questions.key_step: Write x,y,z in terms of a,b for the A.P. (and for the reciprocals in the H.P.): the two conditions give a+b=10 and \frac1a+\frac1b=\frac{10}9.
questions.justification: Inserting means in A.P. and H.P., two simultaneous conditions, solve for a,b.

questions.key_step: Express xyz in a,b for both progressions; the two products have the same numerator, so their ratio isolates (ab)^3.
questions.justification: Products of inserted A.P. and H.P. means in a,b; the ratio trick to isolate (ab)^3 is non-routine and the algebra is long.

questions.key_step: For H.P. roots, \beta=\frac{2\alpha\gamma}{\alpha+\gamma} gives \alpha\beta+\beta\gamma=2\alpha\gamma, so 3\alpha\gamma=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha fixes \beta at once.
questions.justification: H.P. roots of a cubic: key relation 3\alpha\gamma=\sum\alpha\beta then Vieta; two standard ideas linked.

questions.key_step: The last eleven terms are the first eleven multiplied by r^{n-11}, and the terms after the first nine are the terms before the last nine multiplied by r^9.
questions.justification: Block-sum ratios of a G.P.; two ratio equations then r^9=2; moderately routine.

questions.key_step: Write a_n=3^n+b_n with b_n=\frac{3^{n-1}-1}2; the sum splits into a G.P. and a series whose differences are G.P.
questions.justification: Find the pattern of a_n, split into two series and sum one by the method of differences; several steps, exact fractions.

questions.key_step: Convert all logarithms to base 2: the first equation is an infinite G.P. giving y=2\log_2x, and 4\log_4x=2\log_2x=y turns the second into an equation in y alone.
questions.justification: Logarithm G.P. gives y=2\log_2x; second part is a ratio of two A.P. sums; short chain with a quadratic.

questions.key_step: Count the terms in each group and find its first term (by a quadratic fit in part (ii)); then use the A.P. sum formula.
questions.justification: Two group-sum formulas; part (ii) needs a quadratic fit for the first terms.

questions.key_step: Eliminate b using 2b=a+c; the resulting quartic factorises as (a-c)^2\left[(a+c)^2+2ac\right].
questions.justification: Eliminating b gives a quartic whose factorisation must be spotted; proof format.

questions.key_step: X=\frac1{(1-a)(1-b)}=\frac{11}5 by Vieta, and Y is a G.P. in 4\log_b2 with first term \log_b5, giving \frac13.
questions.justification: Four stages: Vieta with a substitution, convergent G.P., log base change, product; exact numbers, no options.

questions.key_step: Square the sum, use a,ar,ar^2 and cancel (1+r+r^2): \alpha^2=\frac{1+r+r^2}{1-r+r^2}; real, distinct terms mean r is real and r\ne0,\pm1.
questions.justification: Rational function of r, discriminant range, and the distinctness exclusions at the end-points; easy to miss the open ends.

questions.key_step: Split \frac{n+2}{n(n+1)}=\frac2n-\frac1{n+1}; then T_n=\frac1{n\cdot2^{n-1}}-\frac1{(n+1)2^n} telescopes.
questions.justification: Partial fractions then telescoping with 2^n; standard method of differences.

questions.key_step: Write the numerator 2r+1=(2r+2)-1 so that each term is a difference \frac1{2\cdot4\cdots2r}-\frac1{2\cdot4\cdots(2r+2)}.
questions.justification: Spot 2r+1=(2r+2)-1 to telescope; one idea, short.

questions.key_step: S_k=\frac1{(k-1)!} for k\ge2, and k^2-3k+1=(k-2)(k-1)-1 makes the sum telescope; the sign of k^2-3k+1 decides the modulus.
questions.justification: Closed form of S_k with a degenerate case k=1, sign analysis of k^2-3k+1, telescoping with factorials; precision risk with no options.

questions.key_step: The common ratio forces a^ab^bc^c=1, which makes the three terms have product \left(a^ab^bc^c\right)^2=1; then A.M. \ge G.M.
questions.justification: Deduce a^ab^bc^c=1 from the ratio condition, then A.M.-G.M.; two ideas linked.

questions.key_step: Split each factor (2^ia)^{1/(2^ia)} into powers of a and of 2; the exponents form a G.P. and an A.G.P. with sums 2 and 2.
questions.justification: Split the infinite product into exponent sums (G.P. and A.G.P.), then solve (2a)^{1/a}=8/27.

questions.key_step: The r^{th} term is \frac{n+1-r}{r(r+1)(r+2)}; split it into (n+1)\cdot\frac1{r(r+1)(r+2)}-\frac1{(r+1)(r+2)} and telescope each part.
questions.justification: Weighted telescoping: numerator n+1-r, partial fractions twice; algebra-heavy.

questions.key_step: T_1=0 gives B=-A; the ratios of T_2,T_3,T_4 then give \alpha+\beta=1 and \alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\beta^2=2.
questions.justification: Recognise T_n as a Fibonacci-type form and obtain \alpha+\beta,\ \alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\beta^2 by dividing equations.

questions.key_step: B=-A and A(\alpha-\beta)=1 give A^2=\frac1{(\alpha-\beta)^2}=\frac15, so A^2+B^2=2A^2=\frac25.
questions.justification: Follow-up of Q24: only the discriminant (\alpha-\beta)^2=5 is needed.

questions.key_step: Shift the variables so that the three factors have a constant sum 63; A.M. \ge G.M. then gives the maximum 21^3.
questions.justification: A.M.-G.M. after a shift making the sum constant; standard.

questions.key_step: Rewrite as 6(x-3)\left(y+\frac12\right)\left(z+\frac53\right) so that the three factors have the constant sum \frac{355}6.
questions.justification: Weighted A.M.-G.M. (scaling 2y+1, 3z+5) with exact fractions; one extra step over Q26.

questions.key_step: A.M. \ge G.M. for x,y,z with x+y+z=60, with equality at x=y=z=20.
questions.justification: Direct A.M.-G.M., one move.

questions.key_step: Cross-multiplying consecutive ratios gives a_2=3a_1,\ a_3=5a_1,\ a_4=7a_1,\dots, so a_n=(2n-1)a_1: an A.P.
questions.justification: Cross-multiply consecutive ratios to get a_n=(2n-1)a_1; recognise A.P.
One substitution into a_1+20d after Q29.

questions.key_step: V_r=\frac r2\left(2r^2-r+1\right) is a cubic in r; sum it with \sum r^3,\sum r^2,\sum r.
questions.justification: A.P. sum formula then standard power sums; options allow checking.

questions.key_step: T_r=V_{r+1}-V_r-2=3r^2+2r-1 factorises as (3r-1)(r+1) with both factors at least 2.
questions.justification: Difference of the cubic V_r and factorisation of 3r^2+2r-1.

questions.key_step: Q_r=T_{r+1}-T_r is the first difference of the quadratic T_r=3r^2+2r-1, hence linear in r with slope 6.
questions.justification: Same algebra plus first difference; routine.

questions.key_step: Group n has n terms and starts at T_n=1+\frac{n(n-1)}2 (the previous groups contain \frac{n(n-1)}2 numbers), so everything follows from T_n.
questions.justification: Four computations from the first-term formula; one needs care with the middle term; matching allows elimination.

questions.key_step: Each part is one standard result: A.G.P. exponent sum, S_{3n} from S_{2n}=3S_n with 2a=(n+1)d, an infinite G.P. inside a logarithm, and H=\frac{2pq}{p+q}.
questions.justification: Four short standard results (A.G.P. exponent, A.P. block sums, G.P. inside a logarithm, H.M.).
